title: The Politics of Grappler Baki
summary: Final part of NH's five-part analysis of Grappler Baki, focused on politics: Itagaki anchors the story in our real world with a working legal system, real countries and humiliated US presidents, which makes the characters' transgressions and strength more impressive. Yujiro's domination of governments raises the ceiling for the whole cast and keeps power escalation believable.
claims: Baki takes place in our real world, shown by its Tokyo setting, real-life cameos, a working justice system and global politics
Armies and politicians serve as the yardstick for character strength; Yujiro clashing with whole countries builds toward god status
US presidents (Clinton, Bush, Obama, Trump) are repeatedly humiliated by Yujiro and Baki, reading more like revenge fantasy than characterization
Because Japanese law applies to the cast, their transgressions feel more impressive than in typical shonen
Itagaki uses ethnicity as a simple factor of division instead of a complex political spectrum, without moralizing
Establishing that Yujiro can take on an entire army raises the ceiling of the roster's power while keeping it conceivable, easing later power escalation
